metadata.title: Some Methods of Speeding Up the Convergence of Iteration Methods
metadata.venue: Zh. Vych. Mat. (USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics), 4(5), 791-803
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available (1964 classic). Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Functional equation $P(x)=0$
nodes.statement: Solve the functional equation $P(x)=0$, where $P$ is an operator (usually linear) from a Banach space $B$ into $B$.
nodes.statement_clean: Find $x$ in a Banach space satisfying $P(x)=0$.

nodes.name: Linear operator equation $Ax=b$
nodes.statement: Solve the linear operator equation $Ax = b$ for $A$ a linear operator from $B$ into $B$ and $b \in B$.

nodes.name: Minimization of differentiable functional in Hilbert space
nodes.statement: Minimize the differentiable functional $f(x)$ in Hilbert space; this reduces to solving $\operatorname{grad} f(x)=0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Find a minimizer of $f$ by solving $\nabla f(x)=0$.

nodes.name: $k$-step iteration method
nodes.statement: An iteration method for $P(x)=0$ is called a $k$-step method if each successive iterate $x^{n+1}$ is constructed from the $k$ previous iterates $x^n,\ldots,x^{n-k+1}$. The same term applies to continuous methods if $x(t)$ satisfies an ODE of order $k$.
nodes.statement_clean: An iteration method that builds the next iterate from the previous $k$ iterates.

nodes.name: Operational matrix and its determinant
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a linear operator from $B^k$ into $B^k$ given by an operational matrix $(T_{ij})$, $i,j=1,\ldots,k$, where the $T_{ij}$ are mutually commutative linear operators from $B$ into $B$. The 'determinant' $|T|$ is the linear operator on $B$ formed from $T_{ij}$ by the same rule as the determinant of a numerical matrix.
nodes.statement_clean: Block-operator matrix with commuting entries, together with its scalar-style determinant.

nodes.name: Heavy-ball / small-heavy-sphere method
nodes.statement: The two-step discrete iteration $x^{n+1} = x^n - \alpha P(x^n) + \beta(x^n - x^{n-1})$ with continuous analogue $\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = \alpha_2 \frac{dx}{dt} + \alpha_1 P(x)$. Polyak calls (9) the 'method of a small heavy sphere' since (10) describes a body in a potential field with inertia $\beta(x^n - x^{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_clean: Two-step momentum iteration with inertia term $\beta(x^n-x^{n-1})$ added to the gradient step.

nodes.name: Well-organized functional (Gelfand–Tsetlin)
nodes.statement: A functional $f$ is called 'well organized' if near the minimum it varies weakly along some 'essential' directions and strongly along 'nonessential' ones; for quadratic $f$ this corresponds to ill-conditioning of the Hessian (large $\mu = M/m$).
nodes.statement_clean: Functional with a sharp/flat anisotropy near the minimum (ill-conditioned Hessian).

nodes.name: Discrete linear $k$-step recurrence
nodes.statement: $x^{n+1} = T_1 x^n + T_2 x^{n-1} + \cdots + T_k x^{n-k+1}$ \quad (4)

nodes.name: Continuous linear $k$-th order ODE
nodes.statement: $\dfrac{d^k x}{dt^k} = T_1 \dfrac{d^{k-1} x}{dt^{k-1}} + \cdots + T_{k-1} \dfrac{dx}{dt} + T_k x$ \quad (5)

nodes.name: Discrete heavy-ball iteration
nodes.statement: $x^{n+1} = x^n - \alpha P(x^n) + \beta(x^n - x^{n-1})$ \quad (9)

nodes.name: Continuous heavy-ball ODE
nodes.statement: $\dfrac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = \alpha_2 \dfrac{dx}{dt} + \alpha_1 P(x)$ \quad (10)

nodes.name: Gradient method (one-step)
nodes.statement: Discrete: $x^{n+1} = x^n - \alpha P(x^n)$ \quad (11). Continuous: $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \alpha P(x)$ \quad (12).

nodes.name: Spectrum of sum and product of two commuting operators
nodes.statement: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be commutative bounded linear operators on $B$. If $\lambda \in \sigma(T_1+T_2)$, there exist $\lambda_1 \in \sigma(T_1)$ and $\lambda_2 \in \sigma(T_2)$ with $\lambda = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2$. If $\lambda \in \sigma(T_1 T_2)$, there exist such $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ with $\lambda = \lambda_1 \lambda_2$.
assumptions: $T_1, T_2$ are bounded linear operators on a Banach space $B$

nodes.name: Spectrum of polynomial in commuting operators
nodes.statement: Let $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ be mutually commutative operators and $P(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k)$ a polynomial. If $\lambda \in \sigma(P(T_1,\ldots,T_k))$, there exist $\lambda_i \in \sigma(T_i)$ such that $\lambda = P(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k)$.
conclusions: For any $\lambda \in \sigma(P(T_1,\ldots,T_k))$ there exist $\lambda_i \in \sigma(T_i)$ with $\lambda = P(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k)$

nodes.name: Operator determinant and spectrum
nodes.statement: For $T$ a $k\times k$ operational matrix of mutually commutative operators on $B$: if $\lambda \in \sigma(T)$, then $0 \in \sigma(|T - \lambda I|)$.

nodes.name: Spectrum of operational matrix via numerical matrix
nodes.statement: Let $T = ((T_{ij}))$ with $T_{ij}$ mutually commutative and $\lambda \in \sigma(T)$. There exist $\lambda_{ij} \in \sigma(T_{ij})$ such that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the numerical matrix $\Lambda = ((\lambda_{ij}))$.

nodes.name: Spectrum of operational matrix of analytic functions of $A$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a linear operator on $B$, $T_{ij} = f_{ij}(A)$ with $f_{ij}$ analytic in a neighbourhood of $\sigma(A)$, and $T = ((T_{ij}))$. If $\mu \in \sigma(T)$, there exists $\lambda \in \sigma(A)$ such that $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of the numerical matrix $((f_{ij}(\lambda)))$.

nodes.name: Norm bound for $\|T^n\|$
nodes.statement: If $\sup_{\{\lambda_{ij} \in \sigma(T_{ij})\}} \max_{1 \le s \le k} |\mu_s| \le q$ (with $\mu_s$ the eigenvalues of $\Lambda = ((\lambda_{ij}))$), then $\|T^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)(q+\varepsilon)^n$ for any $\varepsilon>0$. The same bound holds with $T$ as in Lemma 5 and $\sup_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)} \max_s |\mu_s| \le q$.

nodes.name: Norm bound for $\|e^{tT}\|$
nodes.statement: If $\sup_{\{\lambda_{ij} \in \sigma(T_{ij})\}} \max_{1 \le s \le k} \operatorname{Re}\mu_s \le r$, then $\|e^{tT}\| \le C(\varepsilon)\, e^{t(r+\varepsilon)}$. The same evaluation holds for the analytic-functions case of Lemma 5 with $\sup_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)} \max_s \operatorname{Re}\mu_s \le r$.

nodes.name: Convergence of discrete iteration in $B^k$
nodes.statement: Under the conditions of Lemma 6, for any $X^0$ the iteration $X^{n+1} = T X^n$ in $B^k$ satisfies $\|X^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)\,\|X^0\|\,(q+\varepsilon)^n$.

nodes.name: Convergence of continuous system in $B^k$
nodes.statement: Under the conditions of Lemma 7, for any $X(0)$ the solution of $\dfrac{dX}{dt} = T X$ satisfies $\|X(t)\| \le C(\varepsilon)\,\|X(0)\|\,e^{t(r+\varepsilon)}$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear perturbation, discrete case
nodes.statement: If $\|T^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)(q+\varepsilon)^n$ with $q<1$ and $\|Y(X)\| = o(\|X\|)$, then for sufficiently small $X^0$ the sequence $X^{n+1} = T X^n + Y(X^n)$ tends to zero with $\|X^n\| \le C'(\varepsilon)\,\|X^0\|\,(q+\varepsilon)^n$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear perturbation, continuous case
nodes.statement: If $\|e^{tT}\| \le C(\varepsilon) e^{t(r+\varepsilon)}$ with $r<0$, $\|Y(X)\| = o(\|X\|)$, and $Y$ is locally Lipschitz near $0$, then $\dfrac{dX}{dt} = T X + Y(X)$ has a solution for small $X(0)$ with $\|X(t)\| \le C'(\varepsilon)\,\|X(0)\|\,e^{t(r+\varepsilon)}$.

nodes.name: Convergence of linear $k$-step iteration (discrete)
nodes.statement: Let $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ be mutually commutative bounded linear operators on $B$ with $\sup_{\{\lambda_j \in \sigma(T_j)\}} \max_{1 \le s \le k} |\mu_s| \le q$, where $\mu_s$ are the roots of $\mu^k = \lambda_1 \mu^{k-1} + \cdots + \lambda_k$. Then for any $x^0,\ldots,x^{k-1}$ the iterates of (4) satisfy $\|x^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\|x^i\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}(q+\varepsilon)^n$. The analogous bound holds with $T_i = f_i(A)$ and $\sup_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)} \max_s |\mu_s| \le q$ for the roots of $\mu^k = f_1(\lambda)\mu^{k-1}+\cdots+f_k(\lambda)$.
assumptions: $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ are mutually commuting bounded linear operators on $B$
conclusions: Iterates of (4) decay as $(q+\varepsilon)^n$ in norm

nodes.name: Convergence of linear $k$-th-order ODE (continuous)
nodes.statement: With $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ mutually commuting and $\sup_{\{\lambda_j \in \sigma(T_j)\}} \max_s \operatorname{Re}\mu_s \le r$, equation (5) has a solution for any initial data $x(0),\ldots,d^{k-1}x(0)/dt^{k-1}$, and $\|d^i x(t)/dt^i\| \le C(\varepsilon) e^{t(r+\varepsilon)} \cdot \bigl(\text{initial-data norm}\bigr)$ for $i = 0,\ldots,k-1$. The analogous bound holds for $T_i = f_i(A)$ via the spectral mapping condition.

nodes.name: Discrete multistep method for $Ax=b$
nodes.statement: Let $T_1,\ldots,T_k,A$ be mutually commuting on $B$, $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{k-1}$ scalars with $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i = 1$, and $\sup_{\lambda\in\sigma(A),\{\lambda_j\in\sigma(T_j)\}}\max_s |\mu_s| \le q < 1$ for the roots $\mu_s$ of $\mu^k = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(\alpha_i + \lambda_{i+1}\lambda)\mu^i$. Then $x^* = A^{-1}b$ exists uniquely and the iteration $x^{n+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i x^{n-i} + \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} T_{i+1}(A x^{n-i} - b)$ converges geometrically: $\|x^n - x^*\| \le C(\varepsilon)\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\|x^i - x^*\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}(q+\varepsilon)^n$.

nodes.name: Continuous multistep method for $Ax=b$
nodes.statement: Under analogous spectral conditions with $\sup\max_s \operatorname{Re}\mu_s \le r < 0$ for $\mu^k = \lambda_1\mu^{k-1} + \cdots + \lambda_{k-1}\mu + \lambda_k\lambda$, the differential equation $\dfrac{d^k x}{dt^k} = T_1 \dfrac{d^{k-1}x}{dt^{k-1}} + \cdots + T_{k-1} \dfrac{dx}{dt} + T_k(Ax - b)$ has a unique solution converging exponentially to $x^* = A^{-1}b$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear discrete $k$-step convergence
nodes.statement: Let the conditions of Theorem 1 hold with $q<1$ and $\|Y_i(x)\| = o(\|x\|)$ for $i=1,\ldots,k$. Then for any sufficiently small $x^0,\ldots,x^{k-1}$ the iterates $x^{n+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\bigl(T_{i+1} x^{n-i} + Y_{i+1}(x^{n-i})\bigr)$ tend to zero, with $\|x^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\|x^i\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}(q+\varepsilon)^n$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear continuous $k$-th order convergence
nodes.statement: Under the conditions of Theorem 2 with $r<0$, $\|Y(x)\|=o(\|x\|)$, and $Y$ Lipschitz near $0$, the equation $\dfrac{d^k x}{dt^k} = T_1 \dfrac{d^{k-1}x}{dt^{k-1}} + \cdots + T_{k-1} \dfrac{dx}{dt} + T_k x + Y(x)$ has a solution for sufficiently small initial data, with exponential decay rate $e^{t(r+\varepsilon)}$.

nodes.name: Local convergence of multistep iteration for $P(x)=0$
nodes.statement: Let $x^*$ solve $P(x)=0$ where $P$ has derivative $P'(x^*)$. Let $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ be linear operators commuting among themselves and with $P'(x^*)$, and $\sup_{\lambda\in\sigma(P'(x^*)),\{\lambda_j\in\sigma(T_j)\}}\max_s |\mu_s| \le q < 1$ where $\mu_s$ are roots of $\mu^k = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(\alpha_i + \lambda_{i+1}\lambda)\mu^i$ with $\sum \alpha_i = 1$. Then for any $x^0,\ldots,x^{k-1}$ sufficiently close to $x^*$, the iteration (7) $x^{n+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i x^{n-i} + \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}T_{i+1} P(x^{n-i})$ converges to $x^*$ at geometric rate.

nodes.name: Local convergence of continuous multistep method for $P(x)=0$
nodes.statement: Let $P(x^*)=0$ with $P'$ bounded near $x^*$, $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ linear and commuting with $P'(x^*)$, and $\sup_{\lambda\in\sigma(P'(x^*)),\{\lambda_j\in\sigma(T_j)\}}\max_s \operatorname{Re}\mu_s \le r < 0$ for the roots of $\mu^k = \lambda_1\mu^{k-1}+\cdots+\lambda_{k-1}\mu+\lambda_k\lambda$. Then for any initial data sufficiently close to $x^*$ the equation $\dfrac{d^k x}{dt^k} = T_1 \dfrac{d^{k-1}x}{dt^{k-1}} + \cdots + T_{k-1} \dfrac{dx}{dt} + T_k P(x)$ has a solution converging exponentially to $x^*$.

nodes.name: Heavy-ball convergence for twice-differentiable functional
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be differentiable near $x^*$ with gradient $P$, $P(x^*)=0$, and twice differentiable at $x^*$ with self-conjugate Hessian $A$ obeying $m(y,y) \le (Ay,y) \le M(y,y)$, $m>0$, for all $y \in H$. Then (1) $x^*$ is a local minimum; (2) for $0<\alpha<2/M$ the gradient method (11) converges locally with ratio $q_1 = \max\{|1-\alpha m|, |1-\alpha M|\}$, minimized to $\bar q_1 = (M-m)/(M+m)$ at $\alpha = 2/(M+m)$; (3) for $0\le\beta<1$ and $0<\alpha<2(1+\beta)/M$, the heavy-ball method (9) converges locally with ratio $q_2<1$, minimized to $\bar q_2 = (\sqrt M - \sqrt m)/(\sqrt M + \sqrt m)$; (4) the gradient flow (12) ($\alpha<0$) converges exponentially with rate $r_1 = \alpha m$; (5) the continuous heavy-ball (10) with $\alpha_1,\alpha_2<0$ has a solution with rate $r_2 = (\alpha_2+\sqrt g)/2$, $g = \max(0, \alpha_2^2 + 4\alpha_1 m)$.
assumptions: $f$ twice differentiable at $x^*$ with self-adjoint Hessian $A$ satisfying $m\,(y,y) \le (Ay,y) \le M\,(y,y)$, $m>0$
conclusions: Gradient method has local geometric rate $\bar q_1 = (M-m)/(M+m)$
Heavy-ball method has improved rate $\bar q_2 = (\sqrt M - \sqrt m)/(\sqrt M + \sqrt m)$
Continuous flows converge exponentially with stated rates

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Embed $T_1, T_2, I$ together with the resolvents $(T_i - \zeta_i I)^{-1}$ for $\zeta_i \notin \sigma(T_i)$ and $(T_1+T_2-\eta I)^{-1}$ for $\eta \notin \sigma(T_1+T_2)$ in a commutative normed ring. The spectrum of each $T$ in the ring agrees with its operator spectrum, so applying [Gel'fand–Raikov–Shilov, Thm 4 / property (a)] gives the additive statement; including the resolvents of $T_1 T_2$ and using property (b) gives the multiplicative one.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Direct iteration of Lemma 1: any polynomial in commuting operators decomposes into sums and products, and each step preserves the spectral decomposition.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Suppose $0 \notin \sigma(|T-\lambda I|)$ so that $|T-\lambda I|^{-1}$ exists. Build $S = ((S_{ij}))$ with $S_{ij} = |T-\lambda I|^{-1} A_{ij}$ where $A_{ij}$ is the cofactor of $T_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\lambda$; verify as in the numerical case that $S$ inverts $T-\lambda I$, contradicting $\lambda \in \sigma(T)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: By Lemma 3 we have $0 \in \sigma(|T-\lambda I|)$. Since $|T-\lambda I|$ is a polynomial in the commuting $T_{ij}$, Lemma 2 supplies $\lambda_{ij} \in \sigma(T_{ij})$ with $|\Lambda - \lambda I| = 0$ for $\Lambda = ((\lambda_{ij}))$, i.e. $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Same argument as Lemma 4 but with the spectral mapping theorem (Dunford–Schwartz, p.607) replacing Lemma 2 to handle analytic functions of $A$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: By Lemma 4 (or 5), $|\mu| \le q$ for every $\mu \in \sigma(T)$. Then $\lim_n \|T^n\|^{1/n} = \sup_{\mu \in \sigma(T)} |\mu| \le q$ (Dunford–Schwartz, p.607), giving $\|T^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)(q+\varepsilon)^n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: Lemma 4/5 yields $\operatorname{Re}\mu \le r$ for every $\mu \in \sigma(T)$; the standard exponential bound $\|e^{tT}\| \le C(\varepsilon) e^{t(r+\varepsilon)}$ (Dunford–Schwartz, p.623) then applies.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Stack iterates into $X^n = (x^n,\ldots,x^{n-k+1}) \in B^k$. Then $X^{n+1} = T X^n$ with $T$ the companion-style operational matrix whose 'numerical' counterpart $\Lambda$ has eigenvalues equal to the roots of $\mu^k = \lambda_1\mu^{k-1}+\cdots+\lambda_k$. The hypothesis matches Lemma 6, and Lemma 8 gives the norm bound on $X^n$, hence on each component $x^n$.

nodes.name: Stack iterates into $B^k$
nodes.statement: Define $X^n = (x^n, x^{n-1}, \ldots, x^{n-k+1}) \in B^k$ so that the multistep recursion (4) is rewritten as the one-step recursion $X^{n+1} = T X^n$.

nodes.name: Identify $T$ with companion operational matrix
nodes.statement: Take $T$ to be the operational matrix with first $k-1$ rows equal to the shift block ($I$ on the super-diagonal, $0$ elsewhere) and last row $(T_k, T_{k-1}, \ldots, T_1)$; verify $X^{n+1} = T X^n$ by direct computation.

nodes.name: Numerical eigenvalues are roots of characteristic equation
nodes.statement: The eigenvalues of the numerical companion matrix $\Lambda$ are exactly the roots $\mu_s$ of $\mu^k = \lambda_1\mu^{k-1} + \cdots + \lambda_k$, so the spectral hypothesis matches the hypothesis of Lemma 6.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 8 to bound $\|X^n\|$
nodes.statement: By Lemma 8 we get $\|X^n\| \le C(\varepsilon)\,\|X^0\|\,(q+\varepsilon)^n$; since $\|X^n\|^2 = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\|x^{n-i}\|^2$ this yields the stated bound on $\|x^n\|$.

nodes.name: Analytic-functions case
nodes.statement: When $T_i = f_i(A)$, repeat the argument with Lemma 5 (analytic functional calculus) in place of Lemma 4; the rest is identical.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Set $X(t) = (x(t),\ldots,d^{k-1}x(t)/dt^{k-1})$ in $B^k$; then $dX/dt = T X$ with the same companion $T$ as in Theorem 1. Apply Lemma 9 (in place of Lemma 8) and Lemma 7 (in place of Lemma 6).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Since $\mu = 1$ is a root of $\mu^k = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i \mu^i$ (because $\sum \alpha_i = 1$), the hypothesis $|\mu_s| \le q < 1$ for all roots forces $0 \notin \sigma(A)$, so $A^{-1}$ and hence $x^* = A^{-1}b$ exist. Letting $y^n = x^n - x^*$ gives the recurrence $y^{n+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(\alpha_i + T_{i+1} A) y^{n-i}$, to which Theorem 1 applies.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: $\mu = 0$ (resp. $\tau = 0$) is a root of the corresponding equation, so the spectral hypothesis again rules out $0 \in \sigma(A)$, giving uniqueness of $x^* = A^{-1}b$. Setting $y(t) = x(t) - x^*$ reduces the equation to one covered by Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemmas 10 and 11
nodes.statement: Same as the standard finite-dimensional stability theorems (cf. Bellman, Stability Theory, Ch. 4): use the linear bound on $T^n$ (or $e^{tT}$) plus the $o(\|X\|)$ assumption on $Y$ to close a fixed-point/Gronwall-style argument near $0$; in Lemma 11 the Lipschitz hypothesis on $Y$ supplies existence of the ODE solution.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement: Write $P(x) = P'(x^*)(x-x^*) + y(x-x^*)$ with $\|y(z)\| = o(\|z\|)$. Substituting in (7), the iteration in $z^n = x^n - x^*$ becomes $z^{n+1} = \sum (\alpha_i + T_{i+1} P'(x^*)) z^{n-i} + \sum T_{i+1} y(z^{n-i})$, which fits Theorem 5.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement: Same shift $z(t) = x(t) - x^*$ and reduction as in Theorem 7; boundedness of $P'$ near $x^*$ supplies the Lipschitz condition needed for Lemma 11, then Theorem 6 finishes the argument.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9 (heavy-ball)
nodes.statement: Statement (1) is immediate from $A \succ 0$ at $x^*$. Statements (2) and (4) are the classical gradient-method bounds [Polyak 1963]. For (3), method (9) is the case $k=2$ of (7) with $\alpha_0 = 1+\beta$, $\alpha_1 = -\beta$, $T_1 = -\alpha I$, $T_2 = 0$; the characteristic equation is $\mu^2 - (1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)\mu - \beta = 0$ for $\lambda \in [m,M]$; the optimal-rate analysis from [Faddeev–Faddeeva, Ch. 9] gives $\sup_{m\le\lambda\le M}\max_s |\mu_s| \le q_2 < 1$ with minimum $\bar q_2 = (\sqrt M - \sqrt m)/(\sqrt M + \sqrt m)$, so Theorem 7 applies. For (5), the continuous version (10) is the case $k=2$ of Theorem 8 with $T_1 = \alpha_2 I$, $T_2 = \alpha_1 I$; analysing the roots of $\mu^2 = \alpha_2 \mu + \alpha_1 \lambda$ gives the stated rate $r_2$.

nodes.name: Local minimum and gradient-method baselines
nodes.statement: Statement (1) follows from positive-definiteness of $A$. Statements (2) and (4) on the gradient method (11)/(12) are the classical bounds proved in [Polyak 1963].

nodes.name: Cast heavy-ball as $k=2$ instance of (7)
nodes.statement: Method (9) is method (7) with $k=2$, $\alpha_0 = 1+\beta$, $\alpha_1 = -\beta$ (so $\alpha_0+\alpha_1 = 1$), $T_1 = -\alpha I$, $T_2 = 0$.

nodes.name: Bound roots of characteristic quadratic
nodes.statement: The characteristic equation reduces to $\mu^2 - (1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)\mu - \beta = 0$ with $\lambda \in [m,M]$. Adapting the discrete-time analysis of [Faddeev–Faddeeva, Ch. 9] gives $\sup_{\lambda \in [m,M]} \max_s |\mu_s| \le q_2 < 1$ with optimum $\bar q_2 = (\sqrt M - \sqrt m)/(\sqrt M + \sqrt m)$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 7 for the discrete heavy-ball
nodes.statement: With the spectral bound from step 3 verified, Theorem 7 yields local geometric convergence of the heavy-ball iteration with rate $q_2 + \varepsilon$, completing statement (3).

nodes.name: Continuous heavy-ball: cast as $k=2$ of Theorem 8
nodes.statement: Equation (10) is the $k=2$ instance of Theorem 8 with $T_1 = \alpha_2 I$, $T_2 = \alpha_1 I$.

nodes.name: Roots of $\mu^2 = \alpha_2 \mu + \alpha_1 \lambda$ and the rate $r_2$
nodes.statement: The roots are $\mu_{1,2} = (\alpha_2 \pm \sqrt{\alpha_2^2 + 4\alpha_1\lambda})/2$; with $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 < 0$ one obtains $\sup_{\lambda \in [m,M]} \max_s \operatorname{Re}\mu_s = (\alpha_2 + \sqrt g)/2 = r_2 < 0$, with $g = \max(0, \alpha_2^2 + 4\alpha_1 m)$. Theorem 8 then gives statement (5).

nodes.name: Discrete heavy-ball / momentum iteration
nodes.statement: Iterative scheme $x^{n+1} = x^n - \alpha P(x^n) + \beta(x^n - x^{n-1})$ for solving $P(x)=0$ or minimizing $f$ when $P = \nabla f$.

nodes.name: Gradient method (one-step)
nodes.statement: Classical gradient method $x^{n+1} = x^n - \alpha P(x^n)$ used as the one-step baseline against which the heavy-ball method is compared.

nodes.name: Empirical parameter-tuning protocol for $\alpha, \beta$
nodes.statement: Heuristic for choosing the heavy-ball parameters in practice: start with $\beta = 0$, tune $\alpha$, and add momentum $\beta$ (typically $0.8$–$0.99$) once the gradient method slows; simultaneously enlarge $\alpha$. Decrease both only if $f(x^n)$ increases stably.
output: Empirically tuned $\alpha, \beta$ for the heavy-ball iteration
nodes.pseudocode:
1. Run gradient method (β = 0); choose best α.
2. When convergence slows, set β ∈ [0.8, 0.99] (closer to 1 if slower).
3. Increase α (heavy-ball optimum is roughly twice the gradient one).
4. Reduce α, β only if f(x^n) grows in a sustained way.

nodes.name: Initialize iterates
nodes.statement: Choose initial iterates $x^0, x^1$ (e.g. $x^1 = x^0 - \alpha P(x^0)$) and parameters $\alpha > 0$, $\beta \in [0,1)$.

nodes.name: Momentum update loop
nodes.statement: For $n = 1, 2, \ldots$ until convergence: $x^{n+1} \leftarrow x^n - \alpha P(x^n) + \beta (x^n - x^{n-1})$.

nodes.name: Return final iterate
nodes.statement: Return the sequence $\{x^n\}$ (or its last iterate) as an approximation to $x^*$.

nodes.name: Comparison of convergence rates for ill-conditioned $f$
nodes.statement: For a quadratic with condition number $\mu = M/m$ large, the gradient method needs $n_1 \sim k\mu/2$ iterations to shrink the error by $e^k$, whereas the heavy-ball method needs $n_2 \sim k\sqrt\mu/2$, since $\bar q_1 \approx 1 - 2/\mu$ but $\bar q_2 \approx 1 - 2/\sqrt\mu$. The speedup is therefore very large when $\mu \gg 1$.

nodes.name: Numerical experiments on test problems
nodes.statement: Method (9) was tested on several problems and gave up to a tenfold speedup over the gradient method in most cases; for some problems convergence remained slow, motivating use of more powerful methods such as Newton's.

nodes.name: Frankel's two-step method for linear systems
nodes.statement: For solving $Ax = b$ in linear algebra, method (9) with constant $\alpha, \beta$ was proposed by Frankel; with variable parameters it includes Lyusternik's method, conjugate gradients, Abramov's method, and Faddeev's 'general three-term iteration process'.

nodes.name: Self-conjugate special case is in [Buledza 1961]
nodes.statement: The self-conjugate Hilbert-space analogue of (the second part of) Theorem 3 was previously established in [Buledza, Dop. Akad. Nauk SSSR 1961].

nodes.name: Heavy-ball escapes shallow local minima
nodes.statement: Inertia in (9) lets the iteration 'carry through' shallow local minima: when $P(x^n)$ is small but $x^n - x^{n-1}$ is large the next step $x^{n+1}-x^n$ remains large, possibly bringing $x^{n+1}$ into another basin. A related idea was used by Imamoto–Kumada (the 'golf method').

nodes.name: Practical choice $\beta \in [0.8, 0.99]$
nodes.statement: Empirical guideline: start with $\beta = 0$ and add the momentum term once the gradient method slows; the slower the convergence the closer $\beta$ should be to $1$, typically $\beta \in [0.8, 0.99]$. Simultaneously $\alpha$ may be enlarged (the optimal $\alpha$ in (9) is roughly twice that in (11) for large $\beta$).

nodes.name: Nonlocal convergence for nonlinear multistep methods
nodes.statement: Polyak notes that for nonlinear problems only local convergence theorems have been obtained for the multistep methods of §1; nonlocal results of this type 'would be very interesting' but remain open. For non-quadratic functionals, only very particular nonlocal results are available for the two-step method.

nodes.name: Nonlinear / nonstationary multistep methods
nodes.statement: Investigating nonlinear or nonstationary multistep schemes $x^{n+1} = \Phi_n(x^n,\ldots,x^{n-k+1})$ where $\Phi_n$ is not a fixed linear combination of $x^i$ and $P(x^i)$ is more important but more difficult; only scattered results are known.

nodes.name: Spectral radius formula (cited)
nodes.statement: For a bounded linear operator $T$ on a Banach space, $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|T^n\|^{1/n} = \sup_{\mu \in \sigma(T)} |\mu|$, and analogously $\|e^{tT}\| \le C(\varepsilon) e^{t(\sup_\mu \operatorname{Re}\mu + \varepsilon)}$.

nodes.name: Spectral mapping for analytic functional calculus (cited)
nodes.statement: If $f$ is analytic in a neighbourhood of $\sigma(A)$, then $\sigma(f(A)) = f(\sigma(A))$.
